cues.text: Section seven: secure operations and control design.
Let us begin with the types of controls, which we can classify in two ways: by what they do, and by what kind of measure they are.
First, by function.
Preventive controls reduce the chance of an event happening.
Examples are multi-factor authentication and access restrictions.
Detective controls identify events when they occur.
Examples are monitoring and audit logs.
Corrective controls restore or repair after something has gone wrong.
Examples are patching and recovery.
Now, by the kind of measure.
Administrative controls include policies and training.
Technical controls include encryption and firewalls.
Physical controls include restricted facility access.
Next, three design principles.
Defence in depth uses multiple complementary layers, so that no single failure exposes everything.
Least privilege grants only the access that is necessary.
Separation of duties prevents one person from controlling an entire sensitive transaction.
As an example from the source, a developer should not automatically approve their own production access.
Now let us look at how organisations find and manage weaknesses.
Threat modelling identifies assets, trust boundaries and possible misuse.
Vulnerability assessments identify weaknesses.
Penetration tests evaluate exploitability, and they do so within an authorised scope.
Continuous monitoring detects changing exposure over time.
And incident response involves six stages: preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned.
Finally in this part, enterprise risk management, or ERM, connects IT risks to business-wide objectives.
Consider a payment outage.
It is not merely a server issue.
It can create lost revenue, customer dissatisfaction and regulatory consequences.
That is why IT risk must be understood in the context of the whole business.
Now let us turn to the FinTech scenario.
The LMS describes a growing fintech that uses cloud and outsourced services.
In this case, unsecured communication and missing vendor encryption were discovered.
The key point is that the issue is not merely a missing technical setting.
Governance has failed to enforce responsibilities and vendor controls.
So what would a sound response look like?

It combines several elements: containment of insecure transfers; assessment of the affected data; secure communication; encryption requirements; vendor evidence; access review; staff training; audit trails; and continuous monitoring.
Importantly, you should assign owners and verify that the controls actually work, rather than relying on a written policy alone.
